question: Describe a situation where you achieved a goal with limited resources or support.

raiseTranscript.text: I was asked to deliver a customer onboarding dashboard in two weeks with only one other engineer and no dedicated designer. I broke the scope into a minimal viable version, reused existing UI components, and paired with the other engineer daily to unblock each other.
What did you do when the PM kept adding requests?

I scheduled a quick trade-off meeting, showed the impact on the timeline, and got agreement to park two features until after launch. We shipped on time and the adoption rate hit 40% in the first month.

raiseNotes: Q: Describe a situation where you achieved a goal with limited resources or support.
Role: New grad on small feature team
Situation: Two-week dashboard with no designer and one peer
Actions: Scoped MVP, reused components, daily pairing, pushed back on scope creep
Outcome: Shipped on time, 40% adoption
Quote: "I scheduled a quick trade-off meeting and got agreement to park two features."
Follow-up: Asked about PM requests; candidate described explicit negotiation and timeline trade-off.
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Initiative for a junior. The candidate owned a concrete delivery constraint and actively managed scope instead of waiting for help. Quote: "I scheduled a quick trade-off meeting and got agreement to park two features." The story stays within individual scope, which is appropriate, and shows they learned to negotiate rather than just execute. Biggest strength is the direct link between their action and the on-time outcome without external rescue.

lowerTranscript.text: My manager told me to build the dashboard but we only had two weeks and no designer. I worked late every night and copied some old screens.
How did you decide what to cut?
I just did what I could and hoped the PM would be okay with it.

The outcome lacks any measurable result, making it hard to see ownership or learning. Main gap is absence of any attempt to shape the constraints instead of simply enduring them.

raiseTranscript.text: Our team needed to migrate three services to a new infra platform in one quarter with only two full-time engineers and no extra budget. I created a lightweight migration playbook, recruited two engineers from adjacent teams by showing them the long-term reliability win, and ran weekly office hours to spread knowledge.
How did you get the other teams to prioritize this?
I tied it to their own on-call pain and got their managers to agree to a shared OKR. We finished two weeks early and reduced incident volume by 35%.

Biggest strength is turning resource scarcity into a forcing function for broader adoption rather than just completing the narrow task.

raiseTranscript.text: My team of six had to launch a new self-serve reporting feature in six weeks while two senior engineers were on leave. I restructured the project into four thin vertical slices, assigned each slice to a pair that included a junior, and created a lightweight review cadence so I could unblock without becoming a bottleneck.
How did you handle the skill gaps?
I paired each junior with a stronger engineer for the first two weeks and ran a daily 15-minute sync focused only on blockers. We launched on time and the feature is now used by 60% of customers.

raiseTranscript.text: We needed to hit a new enterprise compliance certification in nine months while the company was still burning cash and headcount was frozen. I redirected two platform teams toward a shared compliance layer instead of duplicating work, negotiated a phased rollout with sales so we could generate revenue before full completion, and used the certification as the forcing function to retire three legacy systems.

We accepted a narrower initial customer segment for the first six months to fund the remaining work. The certification closed a $12M pipeline and we retired the legacy systems six months ahead of the original plan.
